title: Evaluating a statement about a text
examples: How do I know if I should agree or disagree with the writer?
What counts as good evidence when I am writing my evaluation?
Can I disagree with the statement but still write a good essay?

explain.say: Today we will learn to evaluate a statement about a text.

draw.text: Evaluating a statement about a text

items: Formulate your own position (agree or disagree).
Support your position with textual evidence.

explain.say: First we must clearly understand the statement we are evaluating.
Next we need to decide if we agree or disagree with the statement.
Then we must find specific evidence from the text to back up our view.

items: Explain how it proves your point

explain.say: For example, if the text says life is always hard, you might disagree.
In real life, you might evaluate a political advertisement's message.

faq.q: What is the difference between agreeing and partially agreeing?
faq.a: Partially agreeing means you accept some parts of the statement but not all of it. You can acknowledge the truth in some areas while challenging others.
asks: Can I agree with some things and disagree with others?

faq.q: How much evidence do I need to write a strong evaluation?
faq.a: You need enough evidence to support the main points of your argument. Aim for a balance between quoting and explaining the evidence.
asks: Do I need a quote for every point?

faq.q: If I disagree, should I just say 'no' to the statement?
faq.a: No, you should explain why you disagree using evidence. Simply stating disagreement is not enough for evaluation.
asks: How do I challenge a statement politely?
What is a strong way to disagree?

faq.q: Does evaluating mean I have to write an essay?
faq.a: Not always, but it requires you to structure your thoughts clearly. You must present a focused argument with support.
asks: Is this just about giving my opinion?
What is the structure of evaluation?

faq.q: Can I use evidence from outside the text?
faq.a: Generally, no. Evaluation must focus on the evidence provided within the text you are studying. Outside knowledge is usually for discussion, not direct evaluation.
asks: Can I bring in my own examples?

facts: Evaluation requires taking a clear stance on a given statement.
Your argument must be supported by specific references to the text.
A balanced response often acknowledges the statement's validity before challenging it.
Using phrases like 'While the text suggests...' helps structure your argument.

quiz.say: If a statement claims all characters are brave, but you find one character showing fear, what is your best approach?
quiz.why: You acknowledge the bravery shown while using the fear to show the statement is too absolute.

wrong.1: This ignores all the evidence of bravery you found in the text.
wrong.2: This ignores the specific evidence of fear you noticed.
wrong.3: This is too vague and does not take a clear position.

quiz.say: A statement is: 'Technology always makes people more connected.' You find evidence of online isolation. What should you do?

options.show: Ignore the statement and write about technology
options.say: Ignore the statement and write about technology

quiz.why: You must use the evidence of isolation to directly challenge the word 'always' in the statement.

wrong.1: This weakens your argument by admitting the statement is partially true.
wrong.2: This fails to address the core task of evaluating the statement.
wrong.3: This fails to use the evidence of isolation to form a counter-argument.

quiz.say: When you use evidence, what must you do immediately after quoting it?

options.show: Just move to the next quote
options.say: Just move to the next quote

options.show: Repeat the quote in different words
options.say: Repeat the quote in different words

quiz.why: Explaining shows the reader how that quote proves your point about the statement.

wrong.0: This is too broad and loses the focus on the specific piece of evidence.
wrong.2: This leaves the reader confused about the connection to your argument.
wrong.3: This is called paraphrasing, but it does not explain the impact.
